item.title: As Trump and Xi Meet, the U.S. and China Are ‘Shin-Kicking Under the Table’
item.description:
When the United States and China reached a trade truce during a meeting in South Korea a year ago, it helped restore some stability to an economic relationship that was threatening to spin out of control.

The agreement forced President Trump to walk back punishing tariffs on Chinese exports, and made China promise to maintain exports of critical minerals that it had cut off in response to the president’s levies.

Negotiators appear to be preparing to extend that agreement as Xi Jinping, the leader of China, comes to Washington to meet with Mr. Trump later this week. On Sunday night, U.S. officials said that they would discuss setting up a dialogue on artificial intelligence and promoting trade in nonsensitive goods like energy and consumer products when Mr. Trump meets Mr. Xi this week.

But despite the plans for a warm state dinner and other pomp and circumstance at the White House, the truce between the United States and China has been uneasier than it might appear. It has not prevented either government from continuing to take action against one another in ways that have sometimes threatened to upset the agreement entirely. Both nations have blamed each other for violating promises made last October in Korea.

U.S. officials say that China’s exports of many minerals necessary for cars, semiconductors and power tools are still overly restricted, leaving some companies uncertain about their supplies. China’s purchases of farm goods lag behind promised levels. And U.S. companies have also been deeply worried about a series of decrees that China’s State Council has issued since March, which expanded the Chinese government’s power over global companies that operate in China.

The rules restrict the unauthorized auditing of supply chains in China — something that is necessary for firms to comply with forced labor laws — and penalize firms for complying with foreign sanctions against Chinese firms. They also tighten state oversight for outbound investments and mineral exports, raising the question of how much influence Beijing will exert over global business.

American officials have also continued to bar more Chinese technology from the United States, from routers to humanoid robots. The United States has recently accused China of copying American A.I. models through what it has labeled “industrial distillation.”

In June, the U.S. added a slew of major Chinese firms to a list of Chinese military companies. And in July, the Trump administration added dozens of Chinese companies to a trade blacklist related to forced labor.

In response, China sanctioned seven U.S. firms that help companies verify and map out their supply chains, including testing for cotton grown in Xinjiang, which the United States banned because of concerns about forced labor. The dueling regulations have put companies in a bind, since engaging in the supply chain checks required by U.S. law mean they could be penalized in China.

The moves, some say, have been calibrated to fly under Mr. Trump’s radar and not upset the overall relationship. But they are still harmful to companies on both sides of the Pacific, and a reflection of the deep challenges in the bilateral relationship that go beyond any rapport between Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi.

“The overall relationship comes down from the top, and President Trump, Xi Jinping have a very good relationship,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who leads negotiations with China, said in an interview with FOX Business in July. “But, you know, that’s not an excuse for them to do things underneath the surface,” he said, referring to the Chinese.

Mr. Bessent said he sometimes described the relationship as “a water polo match” where leaders were hitting the ball back and forth. But under the water, the Chinese were doing “a lot of kicking,” he said, adding, “if we have to, we’ll kick back.”

An editorial in August in the China Daily, a state-run publication, agreed that it was a “perfect metaphor” but called it “an almost perfect inversion of reality,” saying that the United States was the one instigating the kicking.

Ryan Haas, the director of the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution, a Washington think tank, said there was “still room for shin-kicking under the table,” but “there are limits to how hard the kicking can occur.”

Mr. Haas, at a Brookings panel last week, said that the “gentlemen’s agreement” the leaders had reached in South Korea set parameters around highly sensitive issues like tech restrictions, tariffs and behavior toward Taiwan, but did not restrict the countries’ actions in other areas.

“For the last many months, what we’ve seen is kind of a testing and probing by both sides to understand what can be done competitively while still keeping that leader-level rapprochement on track,” Mira Rapp-Hooper, a visiting fellow at Brookings, said at the same event.

“I don’t think any of us can predict with any certainty how long an arrangement like this could go,” she said, calling it “an extremely unique way to handle a great power relationship.”

Officials on both sides will be focused on positive announcements next week. The United States is pushing for China to fulfill promises made earlier this year to buy U.S. farm goods and Boeing airplanes.

Both countries appear interested in making progress to set up a new “board of trade” that could lower tariffs on $30 billion of goods on each side. And analysts are watching to see how much progress the meetings will make on issues like A.I. safety and the war in Iran, and whether they will address Taiwan or Chinese investment in the United States.

But most analysts believe the biggest focus of the trip will be ensuring that basic stability between the countries continues. China has pushed for a longer extension of the current trade truce, which expires in November, but the U.S. has proposed it be extended for just six months to keep negotiations on a tighter leash, people familiar with the negotiations say.

In a briefing with reporters Friday, an administration official declined to say whether the truce would be extended, saying that it would be on the agenda for the meeting. The official also said that China’s performance in supplying the U.S. and global economy with rare earths had not been up to U.S. expectations and would be discussed, along with topics like A.I. safety and China’s role in the U.S. fentanyl crisis.

The meetings this week could simply lay the groundwork for an extension of the truce, with any announcement coming later. In an interview with the Financial Times on Sunday, U.S. officials said that the trade truce didn’t officially expire until Nov. 30, so it wasn’t critical it be extended immediately.

Sara Schuman, a former U.S. trade official and a managing director at Beacon Global Strategies, said the Chinese would like to see the truce extended for as long as possible, but the United States wants more frequent renegotiations that would allow it to press China on commitments that have not been fulfilled.

“From the U.S. perspective, right now China is just barely squeaking through on its commitments on critical minerals and rare earths,” Ms. Schuman said. “My expectation is that there’s a direct correlation between what China offers on critical minerals in this meeting and whether or not the truce is extended, and for how long,” she added.

Geoffrey Gertz, a senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, a Washington think tank, said there was a “real risk” in the coming months that one side would unintentionally upset the trade truce by crossing what the other party sees as a red line.

“I think over time, some type of that miscalculation, misperception is pretty likely,” he said.

item.title: Paramount Reaches Deal to Clear Way to Create News and Media Giant
item.description:
Paramount reached an agreement on Monday to resolve an antitrust lawsuit delaying its $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, eliminating the last significant barrier to the creation of an entertainment and media colossus.

A group of states, led by California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, a Democrat, sued Paramount in July, arguing that an acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery would concentrate too much power over cable TV and blockbuster films under one company.

After weeks of on-again-off-again negotiations, Paramount and the states agreed to a number of concessions to complete the deal, Mr. Bonta said at a news conference on Monday. The entertainment giant has agreed to establish a board to ensure the editorial independence of CNN and CBS News and committed to distributing 30 movies in theaters every year. The company also pledged to spend an additional $1.5 billion on film production over the next five years and guaranteed to increase the share of those movies that are made in America.

A completion of the blockbuster deal would create one of the largest entertainment companies in the world. It would pair Paramount’s movie studio with Warner Bros., which has made films like “Superman,” “A Minecraft Movie” and “Sinners.” The combined company would also own two major streaming services, Paramount+ and HBO Max, and control both CNN and CBS News.

The deal would make David Ellison, the chief executive of Paramount, one of the most powerful people in the entertainment industry, backed by the fortune of his father, the billionaire Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison. The Ellison family’s ties to President Trump — which included a dinner David Ellison hosted this spring “honoring the Trump White House” — have made Democrats and many journalists at CNN wary of the deal.

David Ellison praised the settlement in a statement, saying it would help attain the company’s goal of building “a stronger Hollywood.”

“Our shared aim was an outcome that best serves consumers, workers and — most importantly — the creative community so vital to the art of visual storytelling,” Mr. Ellison said. “We’re confident this agreement does exactly that.”

Mr. Bonta praised the terms of the settlement but withheld his approval for the deal.

“I want to be clear about something right up front: This settlement is not a vote of support for this merger,” Mr. Bonta said. “It is not a blessing of the broader merger. Broadly speaking, we believe further consolidation of markets that are central to American economic life doesn’t serve the American economy.”

As part of the agreement, Paramount must sell off parts of the company if it doesn’t meet its obligations to produce and distribute films, according to the settlement. In an effort to keep cable TV prices down, the agreement also requires the combined company to sell its bundles of cable channels to distributors separately. In addition, Paramount must maintain ownership of the historical studio lots of both companies, a guarantor that production will continue in California, and operate a fund for purchasing independent films.

Paramount stopped short of agreeing to concessions that would alter the fundamental makeup of the combined company, such as selling CNN or one of its movie studios. The concessions were formalized in a consent decree, a mutually agreed upon list of compromises that resolve the lawsuit. A court still needs to approve it.

Shares of Paramount were up about 4 percent and Warner Bros. Discovery up 11 percent in early afternoon trading shortly after the deal was announced.

Paramount has said the deal is necessary, in part, to create a counterweight to increasingly powerful tech companies like Netflix that are muscling in on Hollywood. Mr. Ellison intends to close the deal in about two weeks, according to a letter to staff obtained by The New York Times. The company has agreed to pay Warner Bros. Discovery’s shareholders $7 million a day if the deal does not close by Oct. 1, meaning the new timeline runs the risk of forcing Paramount to spend millions of dollars in fees before closing. That is still far less than the amount it would have to pay if the case had waited months to go to trial that could last even longer.

Monday’s settlement helps culminate Paramount’s yearlong pursuit of Warner Bros. Discovery, a hard-fought battle with the streaming giant Netflix that required a series of escalating bids from Mr. Ellison. Netflix ultimately dropped out this year, leaving Paramount as the top bidder. The company has spent the last several months fighting the attorneys general in and out of the courtroom, waging a public relations battle and even threatening to leave California.

Labor organizations, which represent thousands of entertainment industry employees, have been split over the deal, with some viewing a settlement with antitrust protections as the most pragmatic option in an industry rocked by economic contraction and technological disruption. But some critics have described Mr. Ellison’s acquisition of Warner Bros. in stark, existential terms, fearing it would lead to widespread layoffs and less competition in Hollywood.

In July, the Writers Guild of America East and Writers Guild of America West, jointly the WGA, filed a separate lawsuit to block the proposed merger, saying it would cause harm to writers and violate federal antitrust law. On Monday, the WGA announced that its members could not alone afford to continue the legal battle and that it had settled that companion lawsuit as well.

CBS News has also been under a microscope since Mr. Ellison last year handpicked Bari Weiss, a contrarian critic of mainstream media, to be its editor in chief. This year, Ms. Weiss purged the senior leadership of “60 Minutes,” the network’s newsmagazine. Many star correspondents, including Scott Pelley and Anderson Cooper, either quit or were forced out.

Some of those who exited said Ms. Weiss tried to inject political bias into the segments, a claim that CBS News has denied. In the aftermath, Mr. Ellison called Lesley Stahl, one of the show’s remaining correspondents, to calm the turmoil and promised editorial independence for “60 Minutes.”

William Tong, the Democratic attorney general of Connecticut, who signed on to the settlement, said in a statement that the state had “wanted and demanded full divestiture of CNN and CBS News” and was “deeply disappointed that we could not do more.”

Norman Eisen, the leader of a coalition of entertainment and news industry professionals who opposed the deal, said in an interview that his organization, Democracy Defenders, would be establishing a new program as a watchdog for CNN, CBS News and the new independent editorial board that Paramount has agreed to create.

“We and our partners will be on the case 24/7 to make sure CNN and CBS News and the new board are held accountable,” Mr. Eisen said.

Other opponents of the deal were less hopeful. The advocacy organization Free Press, which opposes media consolidation, accused Mr. Bonta of “capitulation.”

“Based on all reports, this weak deal contains nothing but unenforceable, empty Paramount promises,” Jessica J. González, co-chief executive of the nonprofit, said in a statement. “It will cut jobs and raise prices, all as it consolidates the media even more to enable authoritarians.”

The states and Paramount reached a deal after increasing political pressure. Paramount had threatened to leave California, potentially relocating thousands of jobs.

After Paramount threatened to leave, Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, who is finishing his tenure in January and considering a run for president in 2028, said he was concerned such a move would be a blow to the state’s reputation. Karen Bass, the mayor of Los Angeles, is locked in a tight race for re-election in a city already facing waning work in show business.

Some analysts had warned that the merger would make redundant thousands of entertainment jobs in the state. Others warned that neither Paramount nor Warner Bros. could succeed alone, and that the status quo could bring even more sweeping layoffs.

On Monday, Mr. Newsom said the agreement was “a practical path forward.” Ms. Bass said she did “not want to see two of Hollywood’s largest studios consolidated under one company,” but pointed to the deal’s commitments to continuing production and its enforceable guarantees.

Mr. Bonta said he had met repeatedly throughout the litigation with “the workers who would be most impacted by this merger.”

“What I heard time and time again is that protecting their jobs today and for years to come is their top priority,” Mr. Bonta said. The lawsuit was “a meat-and-potatoes antitrust case — a black-and-white, bread-and-butter antitrust case — and we got a strong antitrust outcome,” he added.

item.title: China’s Continued Control of Rare Earths Looms Over Trump-Xi Meeting
item.description:
China’s restrictions on exports of crucial rare-earth metals and rare-earth magnets remain one of the most difficult unresolved issues as President Trump and Xi Jinping prepare to meet this week.

For months, manufacturers in the United States, Europe, Japan and India have complained about difficulties in obtaining enough rare-earth metals from China, which dominates global production. The materials are essential for making products ranging from cars and wind turbines to semiconductors, computer displays and military equipment.

China imposed export controls in April 2025 on seven kinds of rare earths and magnets made from them. It later announced a broader set of restrictions, now scheduled to take effect Nov. 10. And in a political dispute, China has slashed shipments of rare earths and magnets to Japan, disrupting supply chains that also serve American manufacturers.

All three issues — the existing controls, the Nov. 10 restrictions and the curbs on Japan — are expected to loom over the meeting between Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi, China’s top leader. There is little indication so far of how they might be resolved.

Rare earths have become a critical trade issue between the two countries since Beijing introduced export licensing rules two days after Mr. Trump imposed steep tariffs in April 2025 on China and dozens of other countries. China’s rare-earth shipments slowed to a trickle, and some manufacturers from elsewhere had to cut output of their products.

The experience last year demonstrated the leverage China derives from its near monopoly on the production of the important materials.

The White House says China has not fully followed through on previous discussions about issuing more export licenses. Deliveries have “not been up to par of what we would expect, and that, I’m sure, will be a topic of discussion,” a senior U.S. official said at a briefing on Friday.

American and European business groups say shipments are frequently delayed or incomplete or never arrive. China’s Ministry of Commerce scrutinizes every export application.

“While most of our members report getting the majority of the rare-earth supplies they need, the restrictions around the sector have given many doubts about relying on China as a dependable long-term supply chain partner,” said Michael Hart, the president of the American Chamber of Commerce in China.

Guo Jiakun, a spokesman for China’s foreign ministry, said on Monday that Beijing remained committed to maintaining stable and secure supply chains for critical minerals.

The restrictions set to begin on Nov. 10 present another challenge. Current and former American officials said the United States and China had discussed postponing the rules but had been unable to agree on how long such an extension should last. They spoke on the condition of anonymity because of diplomatic sensitivities.

The United States has proposed a delay of six months to a year as part of a broader freeze on American tariffs and other trade actions, the officials said.

Such a deal would push renewed trade tensions beyond the U.S. midterm elections while leaving the Trump administration time to press Beijing before the 2028 presidential campaign over its trade surplus, import restrictions and industrial subsidies.

But Beijing has its own political calendar. The Communist Party is expected to hold its once-every-five-years national congress next autumn, when it chooses the country’s top leadership. China typically seeks to minimize disputes ahead of the gathering, meaning a six-month or one-year deal could expire at an awkward time.

China has instead sought a halt to further American tariffs and other trade actions for the remainder of Mr. Trump’s presidency, current and former American officials said. Chinese officials have declined to confirm that position and claim that the export controls are intended to prevent rare earths from being used in military equipment.

Mr. Guo declined on Monday to discuss a possible extension of the Nov. 10 rules.

Those rules would impose controls on five additional rare-earth elements, including erbium, which is vital for fiber-optic communications in artificial intelligence data centers and transoceanic cables. Even before the rules take effect, China appears to be restricting or delaying erbium exports, industry experts said.

“You’ve had bottlenecks building up at several Chinese ports,” said Ellie Saklatvala, metals director at Argus Media, a commodities pricing firm in London.

The most difficult dispute may be China’s sharp reduction in shipments of rare-earth magnets to Japan and its near suspension of some particularly important rare earths, including dysprosium, which is widely used in magnets for cars and in the most advanced chips.

China began imposing the restrictions in December after Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan said her country could help defend Taiwan if China invaded. Taiwan is an island democracy that Beijing considers part of its territory.

China has generally handled the sales of rare earths with each country separately, and it is unclear whether Mr. Xi will discuss the restrictions on Japan with Mr. Trump. Asked Monday about shipments to Japan, Mr. Guo, the Chinese government spokesman, said China prohibited exports of dual-use items intended for Japan’s military, as well as other items that could strengthen its military.

China’s dominance of the industry gives it considerable leverage. Its refineries produce about 90 percent of the world’s supply of four rare-earth elements widely used in oil refining, glass polishing and low-end magnets: lanthanum, cerium, neodymium and praseodymium. Beijing has not restricted their export.

It also produces nearly all of the global supply of a dozen other rare-earth elements needed for a range of products, from semiconductors and lasers to wind turbines and robots. The export of seven of those have required special licenses since April 2025, and the Nov. 10 rules call for export licensing on the other five.

Beijing says its rare-earth controls are meant to prevent weapons proliferation, rather than to exert economic pressure. But military uses account for only a small share of global rare-earth consumption.

The Department of Defense estimated in 2024 that American military demand accounted for only 0.1 percent of global rare-earth demand. But that figure is skewed lower because it includes enormous volumes of common rare earths used in civilian applications like oil refining and glass polishing.

Even when the comparison is limited to the scarcer rare earths most important to weapon production, industry estimates put military uses at roughly 2 to 5 percent of overall demand.

Ana Swanson contributed reporting from Washington and Ruoxin Zhang contributed research from Beijing.

item.title: As Computers Take the Driver’s Seat, Experts Worry About Safety
item.description:
Car software that does much of the work of driving is becoming more capable by the week. But, strangely enough, the better the technology becomes at steering, braking and navigating, the riskier it may be at least some of the time.

Experts call it automation complacency. In other words, drivers may overestimate what the technology can do and become so reliant on it that they stop paying attention and are unprepared when something goes wrong.

That happened recently to Kyle Shanahan, the head coach of the San Francisco 49ers, who has used the self-driving features of his Tesla for years. He dropped his cellphone while driving in Palo Alto, Calif., and bent over to pick it up, thinking that the technology would keep the car on a safe path.

But apparently the system, which relies on cameras, was not engaged, Mr. Shanahan told reporters in August. His car veered into oncoming traffic, causing a crash that left him with broken bones and a concussion.

One lesson Mr. Shanahan learned was that driving “is a partnership,” he told the reporters. “You don’t just turn it over to a computer.”

Most automakers are working on systems that, under certain conditions, steer and brake. Their ultimate aim is to sell fully autonomous vehicles that can act as robot chauffeurs so good that passengers will be able to read, work or fall asleep.

This month, Tesla began offering paid rides in a vehicle it calls the Cybercab, which has no steering wheel or brake pedals. Tesla says the Cybercab can operate without a driver. But it is not yet legal for carmakers to sell such vehicles to individuals.

Self-driving technology has won support from the Trump administration, in part because Chinese companies are also working on autonomous cars. Administration officials have said they are working on new rules to allow models like the Cybercab to hit the roads in large numbers.

Automated driving features have become sought-after options and a significant source of revenue for carmakers. Tesla charges $99 a month for its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) service. The company said it had 1.5 million active subscriptions in the second quarter, up from fewer than one million a year earlier.

Rivian, General Motors, Ford Motor, Hyundai and others are developing their own technology in what Ann Carlson, a former federal auto safety regulator, called an “arms race.”

But none of these systems available are designed to drive cars fully on their own. Unlike driverless taxis operated by Waymo and other companies, they require drivers to be ready to intervene if the software makes a mistake. In most circumstances, drivers, not car companies, are liable for accidents. And no comprehensive studies have shown that cars with automated features are safer than conventional vehicles, experts say.

“There is this irony,” said Ms. Carlson, who is now a professor at the U.C.L.A. School of Law. “The better it gets, in some respects the more dangerous it gets, unless it’s so good that it doesn’t cause problems, which is not true at this point.”

Guy Mangiamele, director of AMCI Testing, a research firm that evaluates vehicle technology, said Tesla had made “amazing” progress with its software, which is designed to guide vehicles to their destination with little or no human intervention.

Even so, “maybe it will take 500 miles or 1,000 miles, but at some point it’s going to get something wrong,” Mr. Mangiamele added. “If you’re not 100 percent aware and ready to take control, you’re going to be a danger to yourself and others around you.”

Notwithstanding those concerns, many people are embracing the technology.

Carolyn McBride of Oceanside, Calif., bought a Tesla Model Y last year after being wowed by the company’s self-driving technology. She did so, she said, despite her antipathy toward the right-wing views of the company’s chief executive, Elon Musk.

Ms. McBride, 72, said that she has trouble seeing in darkness and that her husband has Parkinson’s disease. The Tesla once prevented her from hitting a pedestrian, she said.

“It’s just such a game changer with people our age,” Ms. McBride said. The system is quick to warn her if she stops paying attention, she added.

Tesla recently described its self-driving technology as “a guardian angel for you & others on the road” in a post on X, Mr. Musk’s social media site. The company reposted a testimonial by a man who has cerebral palsy and said Full Self-Driving (Supervised) allowed him to go wherever he wanted, whenever he wanted.

Experts say claims like that are dangerous. “Partial automation requires a fully competent driver at all times,” said Alexandra Mueller, a senior research scientist at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, a research organization created by insurance companies. “Partial automation is not meant to compensate for impairments.”

Tesla did not respond to a request for comment.

People who rely on driver-assistance systems may not understand that they are usually liable for damage or injuries even when the vehicle was steering itself. Except in a few cases, the legal system has not penalized carmakers if something goes wrong, said Matthew Wansley, a professor at Cardozo School of Law in New York who studies automated driving.

Other automakers, including Ford, G.M. and Rivian, offer systems that are more cautious than Tesla’s. Such systems allow drivers to take their hands off the steering wheel on certain highways. The cars use cameras to monitor drivers and may sound alerts or automatically pull over if drivers are not attentive and responsive enough.

But it’s not clear how driver-assistance systems affect safety. Crash reports and statistics often do not contain information about whether such systems were engaged. Even the data that does exist may be misleading. That’s because cars with driver assistance systems tend to be more expensive, which means their owners are generally older, affluent people who are less accident prone.

Systems that clearly prevent injuries and fatalities tend to aid drivers by, among other things, sounding alarms or automatically braking a vehicle, rather than taking control from drivers, safety experts said. These experts consider hands-free driving systems and Tesla’s technology as more of a convenience than a safety feature.

“I have yet to see independent analyses confirming these significant benefit claims,” Dr. Mueller said.

Auto executives disagree, asserting that their systems make driving safer by making it less taxing.

“The biggest danger is actually drivers getting tired,” said James Philbin, senior vice president for autonomy and artificial intelligence at Rivian. “These systems can dramatically improve that.”

Rivian’s system allows drivers to take their hands off steering wheels on any road with clearly marked lanes. By the end of the year, the company plans to roll out technology that will allow cars to drive autonomously from point to point, similar to Tesla’s system. Drivers will still need to pay attention.

“Over time, the consumer expectation of what their vehicle can do is going to go up and up,” Mr. Philbin said. “And we want Rivian to be one of those top players.”

Other automakers have similar systems. Ford’s Blue Cruise and G.M.’s Super Cruise allow drivers to take their hands off the wheel on divided highways. The next step is cars that drive themselves from onramp to offramp.

“Basically you can get on the highway, you press a button and it’s going to do all the lane changes for you, all the interchanges, etc., all autonomously,” said Sammy Omari, executive director at Ford for advanced driver-assist systems.

In 2028, G.M. will begin equipping some vehicles with systems that allow drivers to take their eyes off the road. “Our goal is to get to full autonomy,” said Rashed Haq, vice president of autonomous vehicles at G.M.

But it is not clear when consumers will be able to buy cars that are so capable of driving that the person behind the wheel can completely check out.

Waymo has shown that driverless transportation is possible. But its vehicles operate in carefully mapped urban areas and are monitored by technicians.

Even when the technology is ready, not all consumers will be, said Olabisi Boyle, senior vice president of product planning for Hyundai Motor North America. “There’s still a significant majority that’s saying, ‘I need to trust this,’” she said, adding that acceptance will grow.

Mr. Musk has been predicting for more than a decade that fully autonomous vehicles were just around the corner. Mr. Philbin of Rivian estimates five years before consumers can buy a fully driverless vehicle, maybe less.

But Bryan Reimer, a research scientist in the M.I.T. Center for Transportation and Logistics, contends that those predictions are way too optimistic. “It’s decades,” he said, “not years.”

item.title: How to Handle a Sore Spot for Group Travelers: Splitting Expenses
item.description:
In February 2024, Stasia Maltseva went on a trip through Thailand and Cambodia with a group of six friends, everyone paying in cash and with no system to record expenses.

The cost of street food, souvenirs, group massages and tuk-tuk rides disappeared into an untraceable pit of paper money. They assumed they’d figure out the i.o.u.s when the two-week trip ended. But when it came time to even out the books, “no one had the slightest idea” how much each person had spent, said Ms. Maltseva, a 36-year-old content manager from Amsterdam.

A huge argument unfolded, she said. One friend was under the impression he was owed well over $200, but with no receipts and differing recollections, the friend went unpaid.

“It was a battle,” Ms. Maltseva said. “We joke about it now.”

Not all friendships are as forgiving. From bachelorette trips to family vacations and bucket-list trips with friends, group travel can easily give rise to contentious situations, especially over finances.

In a 2026 survey of 2,001 U.S. adults, commissioned by PayPal, 46 percent said money disagreements created tension or “ruined the vibe” on a trip. Another survey from Zelle, the payments platform, of 1,000 U.S. adults, found that consumers often aren’t fully repaid for group expenses. This can cause friendship-altering drama, with about a fifth of millennials saying they ended a relationship because of repayment disputes, according to the Zelle survey.

Here’s what experts say about why friends get themselves into these uncomfortable situations, and how to de-escalate the drama before it turns into a full-fledged fight.

The most common mistake? Not having a candid conversation about spending limits and repayment plans before they start filling out their itinerary, multiple finance and friendship experts said.

“It starts people off on the back foot because it forces them to have a vulnerable moment about not being able to afford something,” said Aja Evans, a New York financial therapist and licensed mental health counselor.

Danielle Bayard Jackson, a friendship coach and the author of “Fighting for Our Friendships,” said clients have frequently booked sessions with her specifically about navigating the “complexities of the group trip.”

Close friends often skip the detailed planning process, Ms. Jackson said, because of what she called a “relationship-killing myth”: Friends feel they shouldn’t have to explain what they find fun, because they fear that would be evidence that they’re not as close as they thought.

That fear of misperception intensifies when it comes to money. If someone makes more or less than their friends, they don’t want to be viewed differently because of it, Ms. Jackson said. That can introduce friction into a friend group.

“We’re not as honest and direct as we ought to be before we get into these situations,” she said.

For the trip to make it out of the group chat as smoothly as possible, experts suggest finding consensus about total costs, who’s willing to pay what and the repayment process.

For those struggling to start, Ms. Jackson said to think about the one reason you want to avoid the discussion. Then, use that as the opening sentence and tie it to a goal for the conversation.

One example? Ms. Jackson said: “Hey, I don’t want to make things awkward, but I feel like we should have a conversation about money, to avoid any misunderstandings or disappointment.”

For those with a strict budget, it might help to tell the other travelers about the other financial goals or responsibilities you have, Ms. Evans said.

“That will help them understand that you’re not trying to be difficult, but you have other things going on that require you to handle your finances in a particular way,” Ms. Evans added.

On a trip to Japan with three friends last November, Malvina Abbott described a balancing act between one friend with a limited budget and a wealthier friend who required five-star hotels with precise square footage.

It took two months to compromise on the hotel, and they didn’t have a clear plan for how to handle uneven spending habits before the nine-day trip started, said Ms. Abbott, an 83-year-old retired public defender from San Diego. The wealthier friend ended up spending a lot of time on her own.

“Our failure to talk about money issues made for some uncomfortable situations,” Ms. Abbott said.

When planning a group trip, Ms. Jackson said she thinks about advice in “The Art of Gathering” by Priya Parker: Start by asking, what’s the point?

“That helps inform where you should go, how much you should spend and, most importantly, who should come,” Ms. Jackson said.

Once the invite list is set, it can be helpful to suss out each person’s spending habits during planning. For example, Ms. Jackson said she has a friend who enjoys footing a group bill at a restaurant and gets genuinely insulted when others try to pay their portion.

If you know someone isn’t as reliable at repaying what others fronted, ask yourself if you’re willing to potentially lose that money, said Dr. Traci Williams, a clinical psychologist and certified financial therapist. For some people, the loss is worth it for their friend to join the trip.

Frugal travelers should set a financial limit for when to opt out, experts said. If the total others are willing to spend on the trip is going to ruin the experience for you, don’t go, Ms. Evans said. It’s better to deal with the fear of missing out than to get upset with yourself or others over how much you’re spending, she added.

The trip has ended and the Venmo requests have been sent. An uncomfortable amount of time has passed. Perhaps you’ve even sent a gentle reminder. And yet some people still haven’t paid up. How do you confront them without triggering a fight?

Dr. Williams recommends starting with something positive, so that the friend is less likely to feel defensive. That can be as simple as saying, “I really enjoyed our time together.”

From there, let them know why it’s important for you to be repaid. That could be a bill that’s coming due or upcoming plans you need to save for. Rather than a slap on the wrist, this gives your friend an opportunity to help you out, Dr. Williams said.

Resist the temptation to just let it go, Ms. Jackson warned. While it might seem like the easiest option, it could cause resentment.

“Too often people stay silent and make the assumption that this person intentionally has not paid back yet,” Ms. Jackson said. “Then we start to conflate that action or inaction with their character.”

There are plenty of tools and apps to help travelers make sense of group spending. Reader-recommended apps include Tab, Splitwise, TravelSpend, Splid, Tricount and KittySplit. Some travelers told The New York Times that they use a couple in tandem.

Lauren Downey, a project manager from Hoboken, N.J., recently embarked on an 11-person group trip to Italy. She said she used an app called Tab to take pictures of restaurant receipts and track each person’s spending. She then added those “tabbed” meals to Splitwise, which can be used to equally split payments after users log expenses.

“Some people think it’s petty to settle a bill this way, but ultimately it causes a lot less stress,” Ms. Downey, 30, said. “We can’t all afford the same lifestyles, but that doesn’t mean we can’t hang out.”

item.title: What’s Behind Bessent’s Boasts About the U.S. Bond Market
item.description:
In response to worries about rising interest rates and declining affordability for Americans, Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, has repeatedly boasted about the strength of the U.S. bond market. He told Congress last week that it was the “best-performing bond market in the developed world.”

But for many retirees with their savings sunk into U.S. bonds, or home buyers looking to take out a mortgage, the market probably doesn’t feel so strong. Longer-term Treasury yields, which underpin borrowing costs throughout the economy, have risen to a nearly two-decade high, meaning the price, or value, of those Treasuries has fallen.

So how exactly is Mr. Bessent measuring success?

Mr. Bessent, according to a senior Treasury official, is making his assessment by comparing increases in 10-year Treasury yields with the moves of similar maturity bonds issued by Britain, Germany, France, Italy and Japan.

From the start of the current Trump administration through the day Mr. Bessent made his comment, during a House committee meeting on Sept. 14, the 10-year Treasury yield rose less than those five other countries’ comparable 10-year yields.

Looking at more recent performance, the United States is not the outperformer. Since the start of the year, Germany has had the best-performing bond market. And during the month preceding Mr. Bessent’s comment, Japan experienced the smallest rise in yields.

Look beyond the five countries named by the Treasury official, and the U.S. performance is much more mixed, especially in recent months. However, it remains broadly accurate that since the start of Mr. Trump’s second term, the 10-year Treasury yield has risen less than most of its peers.

Bond investors say Mr. Bessent’s claim relies on a narrow definition of success during a global bond sell-off that has lifted the 10-year Treasury yield to its highest level since 2007, pushed down returns for investors and driven up borrowing costs for American consumers and companies. Aside from Britain, the 10-year yield is the highest of the countries mentioned, meaning the government’s borrowing costs are also the highest.

“The way we have thought about it is the U.S. is the best house in a bad neighborhood,” said Alan McKnight, chief investment officer at Regions Bank, noting that it has been a “challenging” environment for bond investors.

Mr. Bessent has been careful to specify that the United States has outperformed “major” or “developed” bond markets when making his claim. Emerging-market debt has outperformed the U.S. Treasury market this year, with Morningstar’s emerging-market government bond index rising 2.6 percent when denominated in dollars. China’s 10-year yield has fallen roughly 0.2 percentage points this year and remains close to where it was when Mr. Trump returned to the White House.

Mr. Bessent made his most recent statement about the market’s world-beating performance while testifying to the House Financial Services Committee, first in response to a question from Representative Maxine Waters, Democrat of California, about declining affordability in America and the steady rise in borrowing costs this year and then in response to a question from Representative Jim Himes, Democrat of Connecticut.

“The U.S. bond market — it continues, during the past month, since President Trump has come in — has been the best-performing bond market in the developed world,” Mr. Bessent said.

Much of the rise in Treasury yields this year has been outside Mr. Bessent’s control, driven instead by the war in Iran, mounting worries about the government’s fiscal deficit, rising growth expectations from the development of artificial intelligence, and the heavy spending and borrowing from A.I. companies.

But Mr. Bessent previously made Treasury yields his barometer for the administration’s success in improving affordability. In November, during a speech to Treasury market participants at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, he again highlighted the outperformance of the Treasury market, with the 10-year Treasury yield at the time having fallen roughly half a percentage point over the course of the year to around 4 percent — a big move lower in that market.

“Lower Treasury borrowing costs mean lower corporate borrowing costs, lower mortgage rates and lower car payments — which all translates to greater affordability for all Americans,” he said at the time.

Since then, the yield has risen almost a percentage point and is roughly a third of a point higher than when Mr. Trump began his second term.

This has been a global phenomenon. Yields in many government bond markets have been rising this year, with some overlapping drivers, particularly the growing worry over the amount of debt that countries around the world have built up and energy-driven inflation caused by the war in Iran.

There are also other measures of bond market performance, such as the total return for investors. By this measure, the United States has outperformed other markets, but investors are still experiencing losses.

An index of U.S. Treasury bonds returned a loss of 1.4 percent for the year through Sept. 14, according to data from Morningstar, an investment research company. A comparable index for Germany lost over 2 percent, while Italy, France, Japan and Britain all returned a loss of roughly 3 percent.

Since the start of the current administration, the United States has outperformed each of these countries except for Britain, which had a markedly higher total return of around 7.5 percent, compared with a gain of less than 3 percent in the United States.

Mr. Bessent also said in response to Representative Himes that his recent attempt to lower yields by repurchasing the government’s own debt was a success, even though yields rose after the intervention.

“There is a counterfactual of what would it have done? And we then proceeded to have the two most successful Treasury auctions that we’ve had in 20 years,” Mr. Bessent said.

While demand from investors in those two Treasury auctions was the strongest in years, that demand came at a price. The 10-year and 30-year bonds were sold at the highest interest rate since the global financial crisis roughly 20 years ago, a cost that will be paid by American taxpayers.

This month, Mr. Bessent goaded the bond market into testing his resolve to lower yields, saying, “I am the house now.” As yields have continued to rise, he has also brushed off investors criticizing his efforts as “terminal bros,” referring to the ubiquitous Bloomberg terminal that sits on desks across Wall Street.

“You used to be a terminal bro, bro,” said Jeffrey Sherman, chief investment officer at DoubleLine Capital, a large bond investor. Mr. Sherman’s rhetorical response was referring to Mr. Bessent’s many years working on Wall Street — a past that multiple investors said still gave him credibility in his current role.

“He is just doing the president’s bidding,” Mr. Sherman said. “It’s falsehoods where you can tell he knows better. It starts to feel like you are being lied to everywhere.”

item.title: The ‘Kid’ Takes Over: David Ellison Becomes a Hollywood Colossus
item.description:
The age of the Hollywood mogul was supposed to be over. Movies are dead, haven’t you heard? Even the grandest studio — Warner Bros. — had started to resemble a relic of a powerful past.

Then came a “kid.”

David Ellison, the son of the Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, was 23 when he arrived in the movie capital in 2006. Hollywood insiders laughed behind his back. He was dumb money to be fleeced, another star-struck rich guy with a checkbook. A 2015 GQ profile ran with the headline “The Kid Pays for the Picture.”

On Monday, after a remarkable, almost inconceivable run of dealmaking and brinkmanship, Mr. Ellison — all of 43 years old — stood on the verge of adding Warner Bros. Discovery to his Paramount Skydance, giving him control of two businesses that helped invent the movie and television industries. A settlement with 12 states cleared the antitrust lawsuit that was the remaining obstacle to the $111 billion takeover.

Mr. Ellison was already an unusual figure in modern Hollywood — a controlling owner who was also chief executive and a hands-on movie and television producer. Adding Warner Bros. Discovery will expand his power to a scale without precedent, spanning a wider range of media than the empires of classic moguls like Jack Warner and Louis B. Mayer.

Even Bob Iger, for all his regal command as Disney’s chief executive over the decades, never combined all those roles.

“David’s about to become the Hollywood equivalent of Superman, Caesar and Midas combined,” Joseph M. Singer, a veteran film financier and former studio executive, said in an email. “He won’t just be sitting at the table. He’ll have extraordinary influence over who gets a seat.”

Mr. Singer had publicly opposed the sale of Warner Bros. Discovery to Paramount Skydance, citing concerns about consolidation-related job losses and the roughly $79 billion in net debt that the conglomerate would carry at closing, among other worries.

“I believe David’s intentions are good and his ambitions genuine,” Mr. Singer said on Monday. “But I remain concerned that this concentration of power is not in the interests of our business. I hope I am proved wrong.”

Other critics were not so generous on Monday. A senior agent and two film producers privately likened Mr. Ellison to Michael Corleone in “The Godfather,” a Paramount film. The character began as an outsider and became the boss, consolidating power with startling effectiveness.

The Ellison family’s ties to President Trump — which included a dinner that David Ellison hosted in April “honoring the Trump White House” — have made many Democrats and a sizable contingent in Hollywood wary of his growing power. His empire will now span CNN and CBS News; HBO, MTV, BET, Comedy Central and TNT; the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services; and two of Hollywood’s oldest movie studios.

Put another way, Mr. Ellison will soon have Batman, Harry Potter, Captain Kirk, Wonder Woman, Ethan Hunt, Maverick and SpongeBob SquarePants reporting to him.

“We vehemently oppose the agreement to allow David Ellison to take over Warner Bros. Discovery,” a campaign called Block the Merger said in a statement. “This is a bad deal for the future of film, entertainment, independent journalism and a strong democracy in this country.”

The campaign was organized by the Future Film Coalition, a nonprofit that gathered thousands of signatures from film and television workers opposed to the merger.

Mr. Ellison settled the antitrust lawsuits with California and 11 other states after months of legal and political combat. The lawsuits argued that the merger would reduce competition in movies and cable TV.

The states relented after Mr. Ellison agreed to concessions, including a five-year commitment to release at least 30 movies annually, $1.5 billion in additional domestic production spending and the creation of an independent board to safeguard editorial independence at CNN and CBS News.

In an email to Paramount employees on Monday, Mr. Ellison said he expected the Warner Bros. Discovery takeover to close in about two weeks. He will exercise control of Paramount and Warner Bros. through his family’s 77.5 percent stake in the company’s voting shares.

“This is the first time since Walt Disney that you will have a family own and control a major Hollywood company with this level of hands-on management,” said Gerry Cardinale, a Paramount board member. Mr. Cardinale is the founder of RedBird Capital, the second-largest investor in Mr. Ellison’s deal for Warner Bros. Discovery.

“There’s a changing of the guard taking place,” Mr. Cardinale added, referring not only to Mr. Ellison’s ascension but also to an owner-operated model that Hollywood had largely abandoned.

Amassing all that power may prove easier than wielding it.

Along with the mountain of debt, Mr. Ellison’s new company will need to contend with a cable-TV business that is shrinking as viewers continue to cut the cord. He must also integrate two enormous companies — he has promised $6 billion in savings — while navigating internal turmoil and political and editorial pressures at CBS News and CNN. Despite owning two major streaming services, Mr. Ellison will still be competing against Netflix and YouTube.

He also faces Hollywood’s most basic problem: how to make movies and TV shows that enough people want to watch.

After a banner run last year, Warner Bros. has stumbled badly at the box office in 2026. It ranks sixth among the seven largest studios in domestic market share this year, according to data from Rentrak, which tracks ticket sales. Paramount is seventh. Each has about 5 percent of the market, compared with 24 percent for Universal, the leader, and 21 percent for Disney.

On Monday, however, Hollywood focused less on Mr. Ellison’s challenges than it did on his remarkable rise.

It was only 13 months ago that he completed an $8 billion deal to buy Paramount, home to CBS, MTV, Nickelodeon and its namesake movie studio. Four months later, Mr. Ellison launched a hostile bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, which had already agreed to sell itself to Netflix. By February, he had outmaneuvered Netflix and had a deal in place.

Twelve Democratic state attorneys general then sued to block the Warner takeover. Thousands of film and television workers publicly opposed the combination. The Writers Guild of America mounted its own legal challenge.

None of it stopped him.

A man who spent years struggling to be taken seriously had become impossible to underestimate.

In the email to employees, Mr. Ellison positioned the closing not as a culmination but as a beginning. “Closing is really just the starting line,” he said, adding: “I’m confident we’re going to build something special together in the years ahead.

“Let’s go!”

item.title: Global Oil Price Drops Below $100 a Barrel
item.description:
The global price of oil dropped on Tuesday on reports that Saudi Arabia was close to restarting a critical pipeline damaged in attacks by Iranian-backed Houthi militia over a week ago.

The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark, fell over 2 percent to about $98 a barrel on Tuesday, down sharply from nearly $109 a week ago. West Texas Intermediate crude, the main measure of U.S. prices, fell to about $90 a barrel.

Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline has been shut down since Sept. 11, when the Saudis said it was struck by Houthi militia.

The pipeline, a 750-mile network that transports crude across Saudi Arabia, from oil fields near the Persian Gulf coast to ports on the Red Sea, had become the kingdom’s primary way of exporting oil since the war in Iran began. Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz had effectively cut off Saudi exports through that choke point in the Persian Gulf.

An extended closure of the East-West pipeline threatened to drastically reduce how much oil Saudi Arabia, the region’s largest oil exporter, could get out of the region. Kpler, a maritime data firm, estimated that a monthlong shutdown of the pipeline could result in the loss of 120 million barrels of crude for global markets.

The East-West pipeline allows Saudi oil to bypass the Strait of Hormuz entirely. Oil instead could be transported via the Red Sea, through the Bab al-Mandab Strait on the southern end of the Red Sea or via the Suez Canal and a pipeline across Egypt at the northern end of the sea, headed primarily to customers in Asia.

But with the Houthis now largely in control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, Saudi Arabia is once again steering vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, analysts said. The U.S. Navy has been able to keep some oil flowing out of the Strait of Hormuz on sea paths close to the coast of Oman, the opposite side from Iran. Recent days have also seen fewer reported attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

The restriction in oil flows and rise in crude costs have sharply driven up the prices for refined fuels. The U.S. national average price of gasoline hit $4.48 a gallon on Tuesday, up 50 percent since the start of the war, according to the AAA motor club.

The rise in diesel prices has been even steeper, setting a series of records in recent weeks. The average cost of diesel in the United States rose to $6.53 per gallon on Tuesday, up more than 70 percent since the war began.

President Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukraine’s strikes against Russian energy facilities for the rise in diesel prices, although analysts say that the Iran war is probably a bigger factor. Soaring prices for the fuel used in trucks, trains and other heavy machinery have prompted worries of a broad acceleration in inflation, driving up interest rates and upsetting bond markets.

Before the war in Iran, about 130 vessels a day moved through the Strait of Hormuz. That traffic has been greatly curtailed, with only around 20 ships per day passing through the waterway in recent weeks, according to Kpler. But to make themselves less vulnerable to attacks, many tankers are traveling with their navigation tracking equipment turned off, leaving the exact volume of Persian Gulf oil exports elusive.

Lisa Friedman contributed reporting.

item.title: What’s Next for Paramount
item.description:
Andrew here. The media industry’s biggest soap opera, the regulatory battle over the union of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, ended with a whimper on Monday.

Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, declared victory after winning several concessions, but the truth is that most were on offer from the beginning. We go behind the scenes below.

Also: We’ve got a scoop on Howard Schultz’s latest foray into investing in the creator-media industry. He’s teaming up with the well-known sports analyst Ryan Clark.

The last major hurdle for the megadeal to combine Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery is gone.

David Ellison, Paramount’s C.E.O., has resolved a lawsuit by a group of states led by California. Now he’s now free to complete a $111 billion takeover that could reshape Hollywood.

How much did Ellison give up? The emerging consensus is not much:

Paramount agreed to spend at least $1.5 billion more on domestic film production over five years and to increase the number of films it makes in America, as well as to release at least 30 films a year in theaters.

The company agreed to set up a board to oversee the editorial independence of CNN and CBS News.

And it agreed to sell some assets if it failed to meet the settlement’s conditions.

But Paramount won’t have to sell any major assets, like CNN. That’s despite Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, declaring this summer that he wasn’t interested in “behavioral” remedies, which are essentially promises to behave.

Also important, Paramount now hopes to close the takeover in about two weeks, which would spare it from paying Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders millions in late fees if the transaction didn’t close by Oct. 1.

Bonta was increasingly isolated in negotiating against Paramount, according to Bloomberg. Paramount had cut deals with movie theater chains and struck settlements with regulators around the world — including Brendan Carr of the F.C.C.

It didn’t help that other Democratic officials in California, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Xavier Becerra, the party’s candidate for governor, publicly called on Bonta to settle. One of their concerns was Paramount’s threat to pull out of California and relocate to another state, like Tennessee.

His settlement meant that others who opposed the deal, including other states and the Writers Guild unions, also settled.

Ellison faces new challenges. He now has to integrate the two media companies, including handling what are expected to be broad layoffs. And the combined business will have some $80 billion in debt, leaving it with little financial breathing room as it seeks to take on rivals like Netflix and Disney.

Watch for more media deals after the transaction.

And expect heightened scrutiny of CNN, particularly as the network joined others in suing the Trump administration after the president barred them from White House grounds.

Air travel in the Northeast mostly resumes after a day of chaos. Hundreds of flights were delayed or canceled on Monday while the F.A.A. dealt with disrupted communications lines, just as some world leaders were heading to the New York region for the U.N. General Assembly. FlightAware on Tuesday reported only a few dozen delays at the affected airports.

Calls for a U.S. diesel export ban grow louder. Republican candidates in tight contests, including one running for a U.S. Senate seat in Iowa, have pushed for such a measure amid soaring fuel prices. The average price of diesel in the U.S. hit $6.53 per gallon on Tuesday, according to AAA, setting a new record. But Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, has fallen to near $98 a barrel on hopes that Saudi Arabia can resume operations at its stricken East-West pipeline.

Volkswagen’s woes continue. Shares in the German carmaker are down again on Tuesday after the company was booted from the Euro Stoxx 50 benchmark index. Its stock has fallen roughly 60 percent in the past five years, according to S&P Capital IQ, battered by President Trump’s trade war and competition from low-cost Chinese rivals. It’s pursuing a plan that could lead to as many as 100,000 layoffs.

For much of the artificial intelligence boom, Anthropic has dominated the enterprise market. Business customers gravitated toward its Claude models while consumers flocked to OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

But Anthropic, a start-up, is now losing enterprise market share to its rival — which could be a concern as it prepares to go public potentially as soon as November, Sri Muppidi reports.

OpenAI’s latest GPT-6 Astra model is clicking with business users. New data from Ramp, an expense management start-up, shows that OpenAI’s models overtook Anthropic’s this past week in share of business spending.

Astra had the largest market share of any single A.I. model last week, according to Ramp, with nearly 19 percent of dollars spent, in front of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5, which had 17 percent.

Astra is cheaper to run than it first appears, because it’s significantly more efficient, Ara Kharazian, Ramp’s lead economist, told DealBook.

“I would say we were majority Anthropic for quite a long time,” Scott Stevenson, a founder and the C.E.O. of the A.I. contracts start-up Spellbook, told DealBook. “That’s starting to shift. The new Astra model is wildly good.”

More companies are trying to remain platform agnostic. Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and others are constantly vying for the top spot for the best models, so it makes sense for customers to stay flexible.

Businesses can use different A.I. models for different types of tasks. Companies can use expensive models for highly complicated tasks and low-cost models for simpler ones.

Anthropic’s A.I. models, for instance, have been particularly strong at orchestrating tasks, or being the “brain” when coordinating streams of work, said Saam Mashhad of EvenUp, an A.I. start-up focused on personal injury law.

Some good news for Anthropic: The overall market for A.I. is still growing fast. Anthropic’s revenue will probably continue to rise despite losing enterprise market share.

“Some spend has rebalanced from Anthropic to OpenAI, but it’s also true that we’re probably spending more on Anthropic now than we were spending a year ago,” said Patrick Wendell, a founder and the vice president of engineering at Databricks, an A.I. data company.

In other A.I. news: Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president, is set to attend the state dinner in Washington for President Xi Jinping of China this week, according to Politico, which cited unnamed sources. And shares in Meta soared on Monday amid evidence that consumers are embracing its Muse A.I. agent.

Wall Street is champing at the bit for the biggest artificial intelligence start-ups to go public.

Until recently, that excitement extended to companies that build data centers and supply them with energy.

But the political backlash against the A.I. build-out has caused some of these companies to delay their plans, Maureen Farrell reports for The Times:

SB Energy, a subsidiary of the Japanese conglomerate SoftBank that has proposed to build the largest data center project in the world in Ohio, had originally planned its I.P.O. for this month.

But the offering has been delayed, as investors question the company’s sought-after valuation of $50 billion or more, according to interviews with four people familiar with the deal’s marketing efforts. So far, bankers have struggled to find enough buyers of SB Energy stock within price ranges the company and its bankers had sought.

SB Energy’s struggles to win over investors come as Holtec, a company serving the nuclear energy industry that is looking to supply power for A.I., said last week that it was pausing its I.P.O. plans indefinitely, citing several factors that have “impaired investor confidence in the market for new public offerings.”

What to watch for: PIMCO and other firms have estimated that more than $5 trillion in A.I. infrastructure spending will be needed by 2030 to support the A.I. boom. If such projections pan out, Wall Street could reconsider some of these I.P.O.s.

Silver linings: Nvidia said in a regulatory filing on Monday that it planned to buy an additional $1.5 billion in shares in SB Energy at a discount, essentially doubling its stake in the company.

And the Nasdaq Composite is back in record territory on Tuesday as the A.I. trade came roaring back.

But red and blue states continue to toughen their stance:

Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, a Democrat, signed legislation on Monday that seeks to stiffen regulation around new data center projects.

Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas, a Republican, effectively extended a moratorium on new data center permits until an electric grid audit wraps up.

Howard Schultz, the former C.E.O. of Starbucks, is getting into the creator economy business.

He is taking a stake in Pivot25 Productions, the media enterprise Ryan Clark, the Super Bowl champion turned broadcaster, helped found, DealBook is first to report.

The deal comes after Clark’s high-profile dismissal from ESPN this summer, when network executives told him his contract was terminated during a commercial break on “NFL Live.”

Clark rejected suggestions that he was laid off. “I wasn’t laid off — I was fired,” he has said. “They’re using layoffs as a cover and a camouflage.”

Schultz will become an investor and strategic adviser to Pivot25. He intends to help the company move beyond podcasting into live experiences, executive corporate partnerships, brand licensing and multiplatform entertainment projects.

The blueprints: Peyton Manning’s Omaha Productions and LeBron James’s SpringHill Company.

“Audiences are increasingly choosing people and platforms they trust over traditional institutions,” Schultz said in a statement. “The barriers between sports, business, culture and entertainment are disappearing, creating an extraordinary opportunity for entrepreneurs who can build authentic communities and lasting relationships with their audiences.”

Jordan Schultz, Schultz’s son, is a prominent sports journalist who runs an independent media company. That experience helped give his father an insider’s view of the sports media ecosystem.

Pivot25 has reached a multiyear Netflix distribution agreement for its flagship show, “The Pivot,” a weekly studio show produced with NFL Films that now has over 1.5 million subscribers on YouTube.

Behind the scenes, Schultz worked with Clark and Pivot25’s other founder, Alicia Zubikowski, the Emmy-winning producer, to secure the Netflix deal.

Clark’s exit from ESPN underscores the shifting economics of legacy media. The network recently poured tens of millions of dollars into huge licensing deals with media creators — consider Pat McAfee’s contract extension, reportedly worth about $60 million. That has squeezed the payroll for traditional sports analysts on the network.

But that hunger for popular sports creators could create an ironic situation: If Clark’s foray into creator media succeeds, could he end up back at ESPN with his own big deal?

Deals

Oura, the health and fitness ring maker, and some of its backers are seeking to raise as much as $2.2 billion in an I.P.O. (Bloomberg)

Silver Lake escalated a legal fight against Carl Icahn and a group of hedge funds over the firm’s $13 billion deal to buy the talent agency Endeavor. (WSJ)

Politics, policy and regulation

A7, a Kremlin-backed fintech start-up, reportedly used forged documents to move nearly $7 billion in laundered money through Standard Chartered, Citigroup and other international banks. (FT)

“U.S. lawmakers urge Trump to maintain ban on Chinese automakers” (Reuters)

Best of the rest

“Bill Pulte Scrutinized Mortgages of Trump’s Political Rivals — and Todd Blanche” (WSJ)

“Coolest thing ever”: The founders of Praxis, a crypto-backed venture seeking to build a new tech-focused civilization, are breaking ground in Uruguay. (NYT)

We’d like your feedback! Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

item.title: Patagonia Offers $100 to Customers Who Help Others Plan to Vote
item.description:
Patagonia is offering customers a financial incentive to encourage friends and family to make a plan to vote in the midterm elections.

The outdoor apparel company said it would give up to 112,000 customers a $100 discount on Patagonia merchandise if they enroll three people in a program to encourage registered voters to cast a ballot in the midterms. The initiative begins Saturday.

Support for the environment has been a core part of Patagonia’s brand for decades, yet the move is an extraordinary step in corporate activism. The company, based in Ventura, Calif., previously bought political ads, campaigned against the oil and gas industry and endorsed candidates who ran against lawmakers who rejected the scientific consensus on climate change.

Ryan Gellert, the chief executive of Patagonia, said he was concerned that many Americans had become disengaged with politics and environmental issues since President Trump returned to the White House last year. Company executives want to “get people off the sidelines,” he said.

“A lot of people are feeling a sense of hopelessness,” Mr. Gellert said in an interview. “We’re trying to cut through the apathy.”

The people Patagonia customers refer are sent to a third-party website where they can check their voter registration, and find out if they can vote early and whether they need to show identification at their polling site. They must then develop a plan to cast their ballot — by voting early, by mail or in person on Election Day.

Customers who made the referrals can choose to receive a $100 credit on their next order from Patagonia, or make a donation of the same amount to the League of Conservation Voters, an environmental advocacy group.

Patagonia said that its goal was to reach more than 300,000 people with its campaign and that it had committed up to $11.2 million to the initiative. The company reported nearly $1.5 billion in revenue during its last fiscal year. More than 60 percent of its sales come from customers in the United States.

Patagonia’s founder, Yvon Chouinard, has been a staunch activist since he began selling rock-climbing equipment in the 1950s, and the company has pledged 1 percent of sales to environmental groups for more than 40 years.

“We’ve never seen a government attack on nature — on public lands, on biodiversity and in climate — like we’re seeing right now,” Mr. Gellert said. “The stakes are more acute than we’ve ever seen.”

Both political parties have poured money into campaigns across the country in the final midterm stretch, with Republicans holding the financial edge. Mr. Trump has also proposed sending a $5,000 check to every American adult if the Republicans retain control of the House and Senate.

Many corporations have been involved in voting-related programs, often aimed at their employees. Levi Strauss co-founded a nonpartisan coalition to encourage companies to give employees time off to vote. Airbnb started a civic action center to help citizens check their voter information. Live Nation has used its concert venues as polling places.

Patagonia has been at odds with Mr. Trump during both of his terms, primarily over the protection of public lands.

In July, Mr. Trump shrank the size of two national monuments in Utah to less than 10 percent of their former dimensions, citing “critical minerals,” such as silver, copper and zinc, within their boundaries. Mining companies were quick to pounce, with at least nine new claims staked on land that had lost its protections from development.

This month, Patagonia joined a conservation group and a Native American-led nonprofit organization to sue Mr. Trump in an effort to overturn his cuts to Bears Ears National Monument, one of the affected areas.

Patagonia worked with the Environmental Voter Project, a nonpartisan nonprofit, to figure out how to approach its midterm push. Nathaniel Stinnett, the founder, said his group’s focus was not to change people’s minds about green issues but to change their behavior so that they would make the effort to vote.

When participants sign up for Patagonia’s program, they will see key dates for the early voting period based on their address and must confirm they are registered to vote and update their information.

“We found a huge number of these already registered super environmentalists who did not vote in the last presidential election,” Mr. Stinnett said. “People want to be a part of big campaigns that the environmental movement is taking seriously.”

The usual selection of fleece jackets and soft-shell windbreakers has already been pushed from the top of Patagonia’s website. Instead, the online store reads: “Vote Big.”

Mr. Gellert is set to announce the initiative during Climate Week NYC. The annual gathering, to promote climate action, is held alongside the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
